        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis.

            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow locally to finish the tasks you described.  
I’ll include the exact file contents you’ll need to create/modify.  

> **NOTE** – I don’t have the ability to run `git` or `ssh` commands from here, so you’ll need to execute the shell commands yourself on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Create Files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo (or update it if it already exists).  
This Dockerfile is tuned for a typical Node.js app that listens on port **3000**.

```dockerfile
# Use official lightweight Node.js runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the metadata files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Tip:** If your app uses a different entry point or port, adjust the `CMD` and `EXPOSE` lines accordingly.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a directory called `k8s` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file named `deployment.yaml`.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Update if you use another registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Adjustments:**
> * If you’re using a different container registry (e.g., Docker Hub), change the `image` field accordingly.
> * If your app listens on a different port, modify both `containerPort` and `targetPort`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a folder `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file named `docker-image.yml`.

```yaml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log into GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Log into GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Prerequisites:**
> * No additional secrets are required because the workflow uses the built‑in `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` which has permission to push to the repository’s container registry.
> * If you prefer to push to Docker Hub or another registry, replace the login and tag steps accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add All Changed Files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-image.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger, building and pushing the Docker image to GitHub Container Registry.

---

### Quick Recap of File Structure

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── Dockerfile
├── k8s/
│   └── deployment.yaml
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        └── docker-image.yml
```

Feel free to tweak the Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, or GitHub Actions workflow to better fit your project’s specifics. Happy coding!
